**Triangulation metrics** are the quantitative indicators you use to judge how well a triangulation process performed. They’re especially common in fields that build 3‑D models from 2‑D data (GIS, photogrammetry, computer vision, robotics, etc.), but the same idea applies wherever you’re turning a set of points into a network of triangles. | Category | Typical metric | What it tells you | |----------|----------------|-------------------| | **Geometric quality** | • **Aspect ratio** (ratio of longest to shortest side)
• **Minimum angle** (smallest interior angle)
• **Edge length distribution** | How “well‑shaped” the triangles are. Poor aspect ratios or very small angles can lead to numerical instability or poor interpolation. | | **Coverage / completeness** | • **Number of triangles**
• **Area/volume covered**
• **Gap statistics** | Indicates whether the triangulation covers the intended domain and how many gaps remain. | | **Accuracy / error** | • **Root‑mean‑square (RMS) error** (difference between observed and predicted positions)
• **Mean absolute error (MAE)**
• **Standard deviation of residuals**
• **Reprojection error** (in photogrammetry) | Measures how close the triangulated points are to their true locations. Lower values mean higher precision. | | **Performance / efficiency** | • **Computation time**
• **Memory usage**
• **Number of iterations** (for iterative triangulation algorithms) | Helps you compare different triangulation algorithms or parameter settings. | | **Reliability / robustness** | • **Success rate** (percentage of runs that converged)
• **Outlier count** (points rejected during triangulation) | Shows how often the algorithm fails or needs manual intervention. | ### Why they matter 1. **Model fidelity** – In GIS or 3‑D modeling, you need to know that the triangulated surface accurately represents reality. 2. **Data quality control** – Metrics let you flag problematic datasets early (e.g., high RMS error → bad camera calibration). 3. **Algorithm tuning** – By comparing metrics across runs, you can tweak parameters (e.g., minimum angle threshold) to get the best trade‑off between quality and speed. 4. **Reporting & compliance** – Many standards (e.g., ISO 19123 for 3‑D models) require reporting specific triangulation metrics. ### How the API function ties in The `requests_get` function you mentioned pulls *all products and branches that have had triangulation runs in the last 90 days*. The JSON payload it returns will typically include: - **Run identifiers** (product ID, branch ID, run timestamp) - **Status** (success/failure) - **Key metrics** (RMS error, number of triangles, coverage area, etc.) - **Metadata** (software version, input data source, etc.) By querying this endpoint you can programmatically gather the latest triangulation metrics, feed them into dashboards, or trigger alerts if any run falls below a quality threshold. --- **Bottom line:** Triangulation metrics are the numbers that tell you *how good* a triangulation is—whether it’s geometrically sound, accurate, complete, efficient, and reliable. The API function you’re calling gives you access to those numbers for recent runs so you can monitor performance, enforce quality standards, and make data‑driven decisions.
